Chapter 1: The Invisible Hand of Luck in Everyday Life
You know, it’s so easy to look back on a streak of wins and feel proud—like every victory was earned through pure determination and smart choices. Especially in finance, right? Picture those crowded offices, people glued to their screens, convinced their brilliant strategies are what make them stand out. But here’s the thing—they often overlook a hidden player in the game: randomness. It’s always there, quietly shaping results in ways most of us never even notice.
Take the story of a trader who’s had a few years of impressive gains. Suddenly, he’s strutting around, colleagues admiring his every move. It all seems like proof of his genius. But what you don’t see? The countless others who made similar bets and lost—stories that just fade away. His success feels like skill, but more often, it’s just being on the lucky side of chance.
And this isn’t just about Wall Street. Think about sports, business, even science. We all love a good underdog story or a tale of triumph. We look for lessons, patterns—reasons why someone succeeded. But what we usually miss is luck. All those little invisible things that tip the scales.
Imagine a parent at their kid’s soccer game, watching a winning goal. They’ll think of all the practice, the effort, the late-night drills. Rarely do they notice the gust of wind, or the defender’s slip, or the random bounce of the ball. Just like in markets, randomness is always there, quietly shaping what happens—and the stories we tell ourselves.
Here’s something to pay attention to: we’re wired to look for meaning. When things go well, it feels good to believe we earned it. And when things don’t go our way? It’s easier to blame a lack of effort. But the real story’s more complicated. Most of us seriously underestimate just how much luck is involved, especially when we look back at the past.
In investing, this blind spot can be expensive. A fund manager who beats the market for a few years is suddenly a star, attracting clients and big bonuses. But if that streak was mostly luck? Eventually, it runs out. You see it everywhere—startups that take off, athletes who shatter records, scientists with breakthrough discoveries. We celebrate the winners and tell their stories over and over, while the ones who didn’t make it? They quietly disappear.
That’s what we call survivorship bias. It’s a powerful force. By focusing only on those who succeed, we completely miss the true odds—and just how much randomness shapes our world.
It’s tempting to think life is fair, that hard work always wins, and skill is what matters most. But honestly? Life’s messier than that. Luck, chance, randomness—they play a much bigger part than most of us want to admit. Seeing this doesn’t mean giving up or getting cynical. It just means looking at the world with a bit more humility, and maybe a healthy dose of skepticism.
